grammar.title: So, Such, So...That and Such...That
grammar.explanation:
Use **so** before an adjective or adverb, and **such** before a noun. **So** makes an adjective stronger, and **such a** or **such** makes a noun phrase stronger.

Say **so** + adjective or adverb: *The banker was **so** busy.* Say **such a** + adjective + singular noun: *It was **such a** busy day.* Say **such** + adjective + plural or uncountable noun: *They are **such** kind people.*

For amounts, use **so many** or **so few** with plural nouns, and **so much** or **so little** with uncountable nouns. **Such a lot of** works with both plural and uncountable nouns.

To show a result, use **so** ... **that** or **such** ... **that**. *He was **so** tired **that** he fell asleep.* In speech, **that** is often left out.

To show a purpose, use **so that** + subject + verb. *She saved money **so that** she could travel.* **So that** often goes with **can**, **could**, **will**, or **would**.

Be careful with two common mistakes. Never say **so a** + noun; say **such a** + noun. And for a result, use **so** ... **that**, not **very** ... **that**.
examples: *You're **such a** good friend.* (such a + adjective + noun)
*There was **so much** noise that I couldn't sleep.* (so much + uncountable)
*I'm saving money **so that** I can travel next year.* (purpose)

practice.q: Rewrite using so...that: The banker was very busy. He could not have lunch.
practice.a: The banker was so busy that he could not have lunch.

practice.q: Rewrite using such...that: It was a good arrangement. Everyone was happy.
practice.a: It was such a good arrangement that everyone was happy.

practice.q: Rewrite using so that: She studied banking. She wanted to work in a bank.
practice.a: She studied banking so that she could work in a bank.

practice.q: Rewrite using so...that: He was very happy. He was offered a job.
practice.a: He was so happy that he celebrated when he was offered a job.
